name: Liam Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Fjordline Electronics Distribution. We sell cables, chargers, speakers and small components to about 180 retailers. I start with a price tracker I built myself, which pulls overnight quotes from factories and flags anything that moved. Then I'm in video calls with sales reps in Shenzhen and Taipei, and by afternoon I'm deciding what to commit to for the next quarter. It's a game of timing and nerve.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when a call on a component pays off three months later. I like building my own little tools, which the younger staff laugh about and then copy. What wears me out is the swings in the market, and being asked to forecast things nobody can forecast. And the pay, which hasn't kept up with the responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief and a bit of a shame. I'd tell colleagues that the tools are good for small jobs and we should use them for that. I'd tell my friends it's sensible not to expect miracles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I built my own price tracker with an AI helper last year, and it saved me about six hours a week, so a plateau suits me fine. But it doesn't touch my money problem. We paid for Sofie's master's and we have under a month saved, and the pay at Fjordline is below what I'd earn elsewhere. There are only two other distributors within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and keep sharpening my tools, because they're what make me look good. I'd ask for a raise on the back of the six hours I've saved the company. I'd also put 150 a month aside. And I'd keep a quiet list of three people I could call for a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable at work, a little tense at home. I like where I am, but I don't love the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money picture at home, since you mentioned the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife, Ingrid, works three days a week at a dental surgery, and that's decent, but not what you'd call a second full wage. Erik's still paying off a loan. If the car gets a big bill, it goes on the card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got worse at Fjordline anyway, what would be behind it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say mostly the way the company is run, not the technology. They keep re-organising and pushing targets up, but they don't pay people for what they build. If someone were to leave, it'd be because they're tired of that.

say: I'd say it's a **relief**, and tools are good for small jobs.
I'd tell friends it's sensible not to expect **miracles**.
think: My tracker saves about **six hours** a week, so a plateau suits me.
It doesn't touch the **money problem**: under a month saved after Sofie's master's.
do: Sharpen my **tools** and ask for a raise on the hours saved.
Keep a quiet list of **three people** to call for a job.
feel: **Comfortable at work**, tense at home about the numbers.
S0.quote: I built my own price tracker with an AI helper last year, and it saved me about six hours a week, so a plateau suits me fine.
fieldNote: He's the **in-house tinkerer**; the plateau suits his skills but doesn't fix thin savings or flat pay.
Blames the firm's habits, not technology, and quietly keeps an exit list.

steps.text: Sharpen my price tracker so it saves another hour a week
Keep a short list of three people to call for a job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's be ready and let's pick the right tools early. I'd show the team my tracker and offer to teach it. Online I'd write about what I've built, because it's good for my name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My team of five becomes a team of two, and I intend to be one of the two. Nobody's offered me that in writing yet. I think they'll keep the people who can run the tools and drop the rest, and at 58 I'm both the oldest and the one who knows the tools best.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put myself forward to lead the firm's switch, which means more work but a better chance. I'd run a weekend course for my retailers on how to buy better with the new tools, maybe for a fee. And I'd put 200 a month away, while quietly looking at what the fees for freelance consulting could be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty tense. I feel like I'm in a race and I'm ahead, but I've also got my ankles in a puddle of money worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Erik and Sofie, about their own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the plan: that I'd be okay, and they'd keep studying and working. I'd tell Erik that his testing job is also exposed and he should learn to build, not just check. I'd tell Sofie to stay in her course and not take a gap year. They'd roll their eyes at me, but they'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleague worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines, the youngest on the team, because she's good with people but not with the tools. She'd be the first they'd let go, and she has a baby. I'd spend a lunch each week teaching her. I think I owe her that, because the cost of this falls on people with the least cushion.

say: I'd say let's **pick tools early**, and offer to teach the team.
I'd write online about what I've built, which helps my **name**.
think: My team of five becomes **two**, and I intend to be one of them.
At 58 I'm both the oldest and the one who knows the **tools** best.
do: Put myself forward to **lead the firm's switch**.
Run a paid weekend course for retailers on **smarter buying**.
Save **200 a month** and price out freelance consulting.
feel: **Tense**; I'm ahead in a race but standing in a puddle of money worries.
S1.quote: My team of five becomes a team of two, and I intend to be one of the two. Nobody's offered me that in writing yet.
fieldNote: He **moves first** and bets on being indispensable; the weak point is that nothing is in writing.
Looks out for Ines, the colleague with a baby, which shows how aware he is of who bears the cost.

steps.text: Lead the firm's switch to AI-assisted buying
Run a paid weekend buying course for retailers
Save 200 a month while pricing freelance work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, but not nicely. At work I'd go to the managers and ask for a decision on who stays, with a plan. I'd say publicly that governments should move fast on support for workers who'll be displaced, because the old rules won't hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the buyer's role is gone in two years. The machine does the forecasting, the haggling and the timing better than any of us. The robots for the warehouse follow about three years later, so the handling jobs last a while longer, but not the desk. I'd say I have a head start, which could be worth something, though not necessarily a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is enough for me to leave the firm with a product and a few clients, but it's not enough to pay off a mortgage. So in year one I'd build a buying assistant for small retailers, and sign up a dozen. I'd ask Fjordline for a consulting contract in return for helping them through the change. And I'd cut spending to essentials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Excited and frightened in about equal parts. There'd be a lot of coffee and not much sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the money work if your plan succeeded, and if it didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd guess 1,200 to 1,800 a month by month eighteen, if it works. It might be nothing. With Ingrid's pay we'd cover the basics, but only if I do something. I'd be telling Erik and Sofie not to count on us for any help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm making it up as I go, and that I have to. I'd say honestly that I'm not sure, and I think that's the best thing a father can say. And I'd tell them I'm going to try, because trying is better than waiting.

say: I'd go to managers and ask **who stays**, with a plan.
Publicly I'd ask governments to move fast on **support** for displaced workers.
think: The buyer's role is **gone in two years**; the machine forecasts and haggles better.
Warehouse robots follow about **three years** later, so my head start is worth something.
do: Build a **buying assistant** for small retailers and sign a dozen.
Ask Fjordline for a **consulting contract** through the change.
feel: **Wired**; excited and frightened in equal parts.
S2.quote: Two years is enough for me to leave the firm with a product and a few clients, but it's not enough to pay off a mortgage.
fieldNote: His answer is **entrepreneurial**: build a product for small retailers while negotiating a bridge with the firm.
Honest that income might be 1,200 a month or nothing, and that his wife's pay is the safety net.

steps.text: Build a buying assistant for small retailers and sign a dozen
Offer Fjordline a consulting deal to help it switch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a deadline and we should treat it as one. I'd show the team what I've built. I'd tell retailers they should start now, and I'd offer to help them, as a service on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 by 2031. I think I could get there if I'm useful, and I'd be useful by owning the tools. But I'd also worry the firm might decide it doesn't need a human buyer in year four. The robots for the warehouse come about 2034, so the physical business survives longer than the buying desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd build the tool the firm will pay for, then sell the same tool to every other distributor on my list. In year one I'd put it in front of three. I'd save 300 a month so I've got a cushion if it takes time. And I'd study basic contract law, so I'm not caught out on licences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish. It feels like a project, and projects I like. There's more at stake than the usual, but five years is enough to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the risks in your plan to sell the tool to other distributors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing is that the firm's data and the tool I'd build are tied up, and I'd need written permission. I'd be careful and honest with them from the start. The second is the market: distributors are conservative and slow to pay. I'd need three paying clients by year three or I'd call it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger buyers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the tools, and learn the human side of the job: relationships, judgement and negotiation. And don't stay at one firm for too long. I stayed twenty-two years at Fjordline, which was loyal and perhaps a mistake.

say: I'd say it's a **deadline** and we should treat it as one.
I'd show retailers what I've built and offer **paid help**.
think: I could reach **63** if I own the tools, but may be cut in year four.
Warehouse robots come about **2034**, so physical work outlasts the buying desk.
do: Build the **tool** the firm will pay for, then pitch three other distributors in year one.
Save **300 a month** as a cushion.
Study basic **contract law** to avoid licence trouble.
feel: **Calm-ish**; it feels like a project, and I like projects.
S3.quote: With five years I'd build the tool the firm will pay for, then sell the same tool to every other distributor on my list.
fieldNote: Treats five years as a **project** with a kill date: three paying clients by year three or he calls it off.
Knows the legal catch, that the firm's data could tangle his plan, and says he'd ask permission.

steps.text: Build the buying tool the firm will pay for
Pitch the tool to three other distributors in year one
Save 300 a month as a cushion
Study basic contract law for software licences

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and that we should start preparing now, not in nine years. I'd say it at work and to my kids. I'd also say that the people who start learning now will have a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me time to teach my daughter Sofie what I've learned, and her time to teach me what I've missed. I'd be 68. I think I could retire at 65 and then do some consulting, which would suit me better than the grind. The thing I'd worry about is the cost of living, and the pension, which would be thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my tools and my usual work. I'd put 300 a month into a pension top-up and into paying down the mortgage. I'd do a side project in the evenings, something like a small buying-assistant for hobby shops. And I'd keep learning every new tool as it appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly good. A bit restless, because I like action. Ten years is long enough that I wonder if I'm wasting some of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter Sofie about her career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's about to finish her master's in data analysis, and she's better at the tools than I am. I'd tell her to work with people, not only with the tools, and to learn a field like health or logistics. She laughs at me for sounding like a careers adviser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most about those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pension. I'm on lower pay and the top-up I'd get is small. If I've got 50,000 saved by 65, that's a good start, but it's not a lot to live on. I'd want to keep a bit of work going until 67, even if it's only a few days a week.

say: I'd say good, and start **preparing now**, not in nine years.
I'd tell my kids early learners get a **head start**.
think: Ten years lets me **teach Sofie** what I know and learn what I've missed.
I could retire at 65 and do **consulting**, though the pension would be thin.
do: Put **300 a month** into a pension top-up and the mortgage.
Build a small buying assistant for **hobby shops** in the evenings.
Learn every new **tool** as it appears.
feel: **Fairly good**, a bit restless; ten years feels long.
S4.quote: A decade gives me time to teach my daughter Sofie what I've learned, and her time to teach me what I've missed.
fieldNote: The long runway suits him; his only real worry is a **thin pension** and the need for part-time work to 67.
Cheerful and restless, he treats time as something to use, not wait out.

steps.text: Put 300 a month into a pension top-up and the mortgage
Build a small buying assistant for hobby shops in the evenings
Learn each new AI buying tool as it appears

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I can't pay off the mortgage that fast and the savings aren't there. What would help is a few months of cover, a proper severance and a public scheme that pays people to retrain. I can hustle, but I need a floor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being early doesn't make you safe. I'm the early adopter in a house with no savings, so every experiment I try has to be a cheap one. I'd like to be bolder, and I can't afford to be.

headlineQuote: I'm the early adopter in a house with no savings, so every experiment I try has to be a cheap one.
portrait: Liam Olsen, 58, is the **senior buyer** at an electronics distributor serving about 180 retailers.
He uses AI **every day**, built his own price tracker, and moves early, but has under a month saved.
He's pragmatic, blames the **firm's habits** rather than technology, and keeps an exit list.
His mood stays uneasy in most worlds and turns **anxious** when AGI is two or five years away.
He'd build and sell **buying tools**, ask for contracts in writing and keep every experiment cheap.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, since the mortgage and savings can't catch up.
whatWouldHelp: A few months of **cover**, a proper severance and a public scheme that pays people to retrain.
